div.p: Many thanks. I shall give your message and press cutting to Mrs Dyer after an interval . (It is always better, I think, to send the whole paper. People look askance at cuttings as if you printed them yourself.) Also, I shall write to Hauptmann c/o you when the book reaches me.

div.note: The face of this postcard reproduces a photograph of a room with a fireplace and elaborately carved mantel, wood ceiling beams, various musical instruments mounted on the wall, and a large stringed harp standing on the floor in the center. The postcard is titled (in three languages) “La salle de Musique. De Muziekzaal. The Music hall.” It is possible that this was a custom-made card showing a music room owned by or associated with the wealthy music enthusiasts, Louise and James Dyer. JJ misaddressed this card to Pound at “5 via Marsala, Rapallo.” Pound’s flat was at 12 via Marsala. JJ may have been confused by Pound’s stationery, which read, “Via Marsala. 12-5.” The “5” referred to the fifth floor of the building.

Louise Berta Mosson Hanson-Dyer, née Smith (1884-1962), was an Australian pianist and harpist, music publisher, and wealthy patron of the arts who founded the music publishing company, Éditions de l’Oiseau-Lyre (Lyrebird Press), in Paris in 1932. Pound wanted to obtain from her an edition of string sonatas by the English composer, Henry Purcell (1659-1695). The “press cutting” may have been an article, by Pound or another, mentioning a coming series of concerts in which the Purcell sonatas were to be performed in Rapallo, Italy, where Pound lived with his wife Dorothy. See Ezra Pound, “Stagioni Musicali del Tigullio: I concerti di Febbraio,” Il Mare, vol. 31, no. 1506 (22 January 1938): 1, 2. (For a fuller account of Louise Dyer, see JJ to Pound 5 December 1937, notes.)

Louise Dyer’s husband, James Dyer (ca. 1860-1938), was a wealthy Scottish businessman who had made a fortune in Australia as an importer of linoleum. He died in Paris on 10 January 1938; his funeral was the next day. (For a fuller account of James Dyer, see JJ to Pound, 5 December 1937, notes.) JJ’s phrase “your message” probably refers to Pound’s request in his letter of 12 January 1938: “I dont know whether I know Mrs D/ well enough to express condolences/ when you see her you might say I have expressed ‘em” (Robert Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 32, no. 3-4 [Spring-Summer 1995]: 573).

JJ had sent Pound a copy of the play, Michael Kramer, by the German social realist Gerhart Hauptmann (1862-1946), for Hauptmann to sign. Hauptmann often spent the winter months in Rapallo, where Pound had lived with his wife Dorothy since 1924-1925. (For more details, see JJ to Pound 5 December 1937, notes.)
